# Agentic AI and outbreak modelling

## What I mean by an agent

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
A language model with tools. It reads files, writes code, runs it, and loops until a check passes
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/keynote-agent-1.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="A brick box on the left, you, the task and what counts as right,
sends a prompt into a loop of four boxes, read the files and the docs,
write or change code, run it, check passed. No returns to the top. Yes
leads to a pull request and a brick box, you, read it, merge or send
back."}
:::
::::

## How I am working at the moment

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- I was travelling for summer schools, teaching and workshops, so made
  a very focused go of working through agents only.
- All code and most text I have produced in the last six months has been agent
  written, pushed from a bot account, a second GitHub login
- Agents write the tasks, from a spec or from a conversation with me
- I am reviewing at different levels. Sometimes all the code, sometimes only the
  outcome.
- My agent is also interacting frequently with Sebastian Funk's who is working in a similar way.

## Agents in the Bundibugyo DRC outbreak model model: the data

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- The situation reports are French PDFs. Agents read every stream from
  them.
- Where available results are cross-checked against INRB-UMIE transcription
- Recent reports get two blind reads.
- Symptom onset data is reported only as a figure in the report.
- We use a agent written digitiser to recover counts
  from pixel colour and axis tick geometry
- These are cross checked again using multiple agents and using digistiers written in both Python and Julia.
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/keynote-bvd-sitrep087-page3.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Page 3 of INSP situation report 87, in French. A table of alerts
by province, a bar chart of confirmed cases by date of symptom onset
over 21 days, and a map of cases by health zone."}

::: {.attribution}
INSP SitRep 087, 9 August 2026, page 3,
[insp.cd](https://insp.cd/ebola-17eme-epidemie/)
· `data/README.md` and `scripts/README.md` in [BVDOutbreakSize][bvd-repo],
read 12 September 2026; the onset reporting triangle fit merged
27 July 2026
:::
:::

## Agents in the Bundibugyo DRC outbreak model: the model

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Model development through issues and pull requests. 333 of 425 pull
  requests from the bot account
- Model structure and approaches specificed by me at a high level.
- Automated performance work by agents, reviewed by agents. 19 perf commits, all
  from bot identities. One review found nothing worth shipping. One
  halved the gradient cost 
- We used agents to manage two versions of the model in tandem. The original integral version of the model
and its renewal process successor. 
- Agents kept the two in step until it merged on 9 June 2026
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/keynote-agent-2.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="The agent loop again, now fed by a box where agents write the
tasks from a spec or a conversation, with review agents sending findings
back into the loop, me reading all the code or only the outcome, and a
merge that refits in CI and sends new tasks back to the top."}

::: {.attribution}
[BVDOutbreakSize][bvd-repo]: pull request counts from the GitHub search
API, 11 September 2026 · `git log --grep perf`, issue #444, pull request
#656 · the renewal model, pull request
[#155](https://github.com/epiforecasts/BVDOutbreakSize/pull/155)

## What agents made possible

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- The original report replicated the McCabe et al. Imperial report over a few hours.
- In a few more issues with that report were addressed and it was exanded to jointly fit all the data streams they used.
- Going wide. One posterior over 5+ situation report streams,
  Uganda export data and a genomic bounding model.
- Checks on every rebuild.
- Following the Infectious disease modelling Bayesian workflow TODO: Needs two refs
- This includes: predictive checks per stream, forecasts
  scored against later data the McCabe replication
- That much debugging would not have happened by hand. The workflow is
  what kept it reviewable.
- Agents did not choose the model.
- Infrastructure and review were still needed to keep the agents in check.
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/keynote-workflow-agents.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="The six-step workflow, question, data, model, fit, check and
report, with a tag over each. People over question; agents read and
digitise over data; people choose, agents write over model; agents,
every push over fit; agents run, people judge over check; agents draft,
people sign over report."}

::: {.attribution}
README and `docs/src/news.md` of [BVDOutbreakSize][bvd-repo], read
12 September 2026 · [A workflow for infectious disease modelling][wf],
Abbott et al.
:::
:::
::::

## Agents that search over models

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- For the Bundibugyo model this was ad hoc. Agents proposed patches to
  the model as issues, one branch each, and every release scored the
  forecast against later data and was reviewed based on domain knowledge.
- The systematic version where there is a known target is a tree search or embedded inference step (i.e. MCMC proposal in model space)
- An agent proposes candidate models, one loop each, fit and score, keep the best, branch again
- How to enforce domain knowledge and how to identify the evaluation targets.
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/keynote-agent-3.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="A tree. The current model at the root branches into three
candidates, add a stream, change the delay prior, and split Rt by
province. Two are kept and branch again into three each; one child of
each is kept in teal and the rest are grey, and the kept branches meet
at a box reading keep the best, branch again."}

::: {.attribution}
Open `patch model` issues from `seabbs-bot` in [BVDOutbreakSize][bvd-repo],
11 September 2026, and the forecast scoring in `src/scoring.jl`
:::
:::
::::

## Google SAI in the CDC hubs

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Martinson et al. 2026. An LLM-guided tree search that writes
  forecasting code. An ensemble of the survivors went to the FluSight,
  COVID-19 and RSV hubs
- It is somewhat limited as it in effect mutates and composes existing domain developed models rather than starting from scratch.
- Prospective, 2025/26 season. It matched or beat the CDC hub ensembles
  and topped the leader board TODO check it topped the leaderboard
- Bracher and Funk 2026. The earlier claimed retrospective gain of 11% came
  from data revisions leaking into the evaluation
- Unclear how optimised other model submissions where and difference in compute and person power used vs other teams is huge.
- The hubs, the data, the target for evaluation and the review of output were still built by people
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/keynote-sai-arxiv.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="The arXiv abstract page for Prospective multi-pathogen disease
forecasting using autonomous LLM-guided tree search, by Martinson,
Brenner, Plomecka, Williams, Reich and Shamsi, submitted 15 May 2026."}

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; margin-top: 0.4em; margin-bottom: 0.9em;"}
The people modelling outbreaks where outbreaks happen are the least
likely to have paid access.
:::

- A Claude Max subscription. £200 a month, from my own pocket.
